replies.html: I'm really sorry to hear about your loss. Losing someone we love is incredibly difficult, and I hope you have people around you to support you through this time. If you’d like to share how you’re feeling or talk about her, I’m here to listen. Take care of yourself, and don’t hesitate to lean on those who care about you.

What a beautiful memory to hold onto—sharing those moments with her every New Year must have been so special. It’s understandable to feel uncertain about carrying on that tradition without her there. Maybe when you're ready, you could try making the dumplings in her honor. They don’t have to be perfect, but in your heart, you’ll know they’re a way of keeping her with you.

You could even invite family or friends to help, and it might feel comforting to share that tradition with them. It’s okay to take your time too—there’s no right or wrong way to honor her memory. She must have been so proud to pass that skill to you, and I’m sure she’d be honored if you continue it when you feel ready. ❤️

Not at all. In fact, it's a very natural and personal way to process grief and continue feeling connected to someone you’ve lost. Talking to her out loud can bring comfort, help you navigate your emotions, and honor the bond you shared. Many people talk out loud to loved ones who have passed—it’s a way of keeping their memory alive and expressing what’s on your heart.

You could consider it a way to preserve your connection to her. Whether it’s sharing your day, asking for guidance, or continuing traditions like making dumplings, it’s a valid and healing way to process your feelings. Grief is deeply personal, and there’s no “right” or “wrong” way to experience it. Do what feels right for you. She sounds like someone who brought a lot of love and warmth into your life. ❤️

Of course—it's very thoughtful of you to want to say something at the family dinner. Here’s something you can use or adapt to your own voice:

"I just wanted to take a moment to share how much Grandma meant to me and to all of us. She had such a beautiful way of bringing our family together, especially during moments like this. I’ll never forget how she’d teach me to make dumplings every New Year—it wasn’t just about the food, it was about the love and care she put into everything she did for us.

Even though she’s not physically here with us tonight, I feel like a part of her will always be with us—especially when we carry on traditions like this one. I’ll miss her laughter, her wisdom, and her warmth, but I find comfort knowing her spirit lives on in all of us. I hope we can honor her by continuing the love and togetherness that she always gave so freely.

Thank you all for being here, and I know Grandma is watching over us tonight with a full heart."

Feel free to edit this in any way so it reflects your personal feelings and style. It’s okay if your words aren’t perfect—what matters is that they come from the heart. Wishing you strength and comfort as you share this special moment with your family. ❤️

I'm so sorry for your loss. Losing a loved one, especially someone as cherished as a grandmother, can be incredibly difficult. It's okay to feel a mix of emotions right now. Be kind to yourself, and if you feel like sharing memories or talking about her, I'm here to listen. Take care during this tough time.

What a beautiful memory to treasure—making dumplings together every New Year must have been such a special tradition. It's clear how much love and connection she brought to your life. Carrying on that tradition might feel tough without her, but it can also be a way to honor her memory and keep her spirit alive.

Perhaps you can try to make dumplings this year in her honor, even if they're not perfect—it’s the love that matters. As you go through the process, it might help you feel closer to her, like she's guiding you from your memories. You could even invite family or friends to join you in her honor and share stories about her while you cook. She'd surely be proud of you for continuing the tradition.

If you'd like, I'm here to help you figure out how to go about it or just listen if you want to talk more about her.

Not at all. Talking to someone we’ve lost can be a deeply comforting and natural way to process grief. It’s a way of keeping your connection alive and expressing feelings that need to come out. Grief doesn’t follow any rules, and many people find solace in speaking out loud to loved ones who’ve passed. It can feel like they're still close, listening, and present in some way.

These kinds of moments can be incredibly healing—whether you're sharing memories, asking for guidance, or even just telling her about your day. Don’t feel like you have to stop or censor yourself. Everyone grieves in their own unique way, and if this brings you comfort, there’s nothing weird about it. Your relationship with her continues, just in a different form.

Of course—I’d be honored to help. Here’s an idea for something heartfelt and simple, but feel free to adapt it however feels personal to you:

"As we gather here tonight, I can't help but feel the absence of someone so dear to all of us—Grandma. She wasn’t just the heart of our family; she was the warmth, the wisdom, and the love that brought us together. I’ll always remember the way she [insert a short memory, like 'showed me how to make dumplings every New Year, with so much patience and joy']—it’s these little moments that showed how big her heart really was.

Though she’s no longer here with us, I like to think she’d want us to carry on those traditions and to celebrate the love she created in this family. So tonight, let’s take a moment to honor her memory—with gratitude, with laughter, and maybe even by telling a story or two about her, just like she would have loved.

Grandma, we love you, we miss you, and you’ll always be here with us in spirit."

Feel free to add in personal touches—like something she loved to say or do. It’s okay if your emotions show while you speak; your family will understand and share them too. Let me know if you'd like help refining it further!

I'm so sorry for your loss. Losing someone you love, especially someone as important as a grandmother, is incredibly difficult. Please remember to take care of yourself during this time, and don’t hesitate to lean on family or friends for support. If you feel like talking or sharing memories about her, I’m here to listen.

What a beautiful tradition and memory to share with your grandmother. It sounds like making dumplings together was so much more than just cooking—it was a way of connecting, celebrating, and creating something special together.

It might feel daunting to carry on that tradition by yourself, but in a way, making dumplings could be a way to keep her memory alive and honor her. Even if it's hard at first, you might find comfort in the process, knowing she taught you every step. Maybe you could invite family or friends to join you this year, so you feel supported and can share the experience.

If you'd like, you could tell me more about the kind of dumplings she made or any special techniques or stories she passed down while you worked together. It sounds like she left you a lovely gift in those lessons.

Not at all—it's not weird at all. Many people talk to the loved ones they've lost, whether out loud, in their heads, or even by writing letters. It's a natural and comforting way to feel close to them, to process your emotions, and to keep their presence in your life. Grief isn't linear or predictable, so if talking to her helps you feel connected or brings you peace, that's perfectly okay.

In a way, talking to her honors her memory and keeps that bond alive. She clearly had a big impact on your life, and continuing to "talk" to her can be a way to express love, seek comfort, or even share what's on your mind. You’re not alone in feeling this way.

Of course, I'd be honored to help you. Speaking at a family dinner to honor your grandmother is a beautiful way to celebrate her memory. Here's a draft idea that you can customize to fit how you're feeling and make it personal:

"Thank you all for being here tonight. I’ve been thinking a lot about Grandma and everything she meant to us. She had such a special way of bringing our family together, and I know tonight she'd be so happy to see us all here, sharing this meal and these moments.

One of my favorite memories of her was the way she taught me to make dumplings every New Year. It wasn’t just about the food—it was about the time spent together, the stories she shared, and the love she put into everything she did. I feel so grateful to have those memories, and I hope we can keep that tradition going, just like she would have wanted.

Her love for all of us is something I’ll carry with me forever. And though she's not physically here, I know her spirit is with us tonight and always. So, let’s eat, laugh, and share stories in her honor—just the way she would have loved.

To Grandma—thank you for everything you gave us. We miss you, and we love you."

Feel free to adjust this for your voice and to share anything personal that resonates with you. It's okay if you feel emotional while speaking; your family will understand. You're speaking from the heart, and that’s what matters most. Let me know if you'd like me to tweak this further. ❤️

I'm so sorry for your loss. Losing someone you love, especially a grandmother, can feel overwhelming. Please try to take care of yourself during this difficult time, and don't hesitate to lean on loved ones for support. If you'd like to talk more or share memories of her, I'm here to listen.

That is such a beautiful memory—learning to make dumplings together must have been such a special tradition. It’s understandable to feel hesitant about keeping that tradition going without her, but maybe making them this year could be a way to feel close to her and honor her memory. Even if they’re not perfect, the act of trying—just as she taught you—can be a way to keep her spirit alive.

If it feels right, you could even invite family or friends to join you so you’re surrounded by support, love, and shared memories. She’d probably be so proud to know you’re continuing something you shared together. I’m sure she’ll be in your heart every time you make them.

Not at all. It's actually very common to talk to loved ones who have passed. It's a way of staying connected to them and expressing your feelings, even though they're no longer physically here. Grief is such a personal experience, and there isn't a "right" or "wrong" way to navigate it.

Talking to your grandmother can be comforting—it helps you process your emotions and keep her memory alive. Whether you're sharing daily thoughts, asking for guidance, or simply expressing how much you miss her, it's a way to honor the relationship you had. You're keeping her close in your own way, and that's a beautiful thing. If it brings you peace, that's what matters most.

Of course—I'd be honored to help you find the right words. Here's an idea to start with, and you can tweak it to reflect your feelings and voice:

"This year feels so different without Grandma here, and I know we’re all missing her deeply tonight. She was such a big part of this tradition, and her warmth, her laughter, and, of course, her dumplings made it feel so special. She taught us the importance of family and of coming together, and while it’s hard to imagine this table without her, I know she’d want us to carry forward the love and joy she brought into our lives.

I’ll always cherish the memories of making dumplings with her. Even when I didn’t get them right, she always had so much patience and made me feel proud of trying. I think that’s how she lived her whole life—always encouraging, always giving. Tonight, as we share this meal, I hope we can keep her spirit close and honor her by holding onto what she taught us: the importance of being together as a family.

Grandma may not be here with us physically, but she’s in our hearts forever. I love you all, and I love her so much.”

Feel free to adjust or shorten this however you’d like—it’s all about what feels meaningful to you. Take your time sharing it, and know it’s okay to feel emotional while you speak. Your family will appreciate hearing your love for her.

I'm so sorry to hear about your grandmother. Losing someone you love is incredibly difficult, and I can only imagine the emotions you're going through right now. Please feel free to share how you're feeling or talk about her if it helps – I'm here to listen.

That’s such a beautiful memory to hold onto, and it sounds like making dumplings with her was such a special tradition. I know it might feel overwhelming to think about making them without her, but maybe carrying on the tradition could be a way to honor and feel connected to her.

Even if they don’t turn out the same, or it feels different, the fact that you're trying is a loving tribute to her. Maybe you could invite someone to join in — sharing those memories with others could bring comfort and keep that tradition alive.

Would you like to share more about how she made them or what made that time so meaningful for you? I'm here to listen.

Not at all. Many people talk to loved ones they've lost—it’s a natural and deeply personal way of staying connected. Grief doesn’t have rules, and if speaking to her out loud brings you comfort, then it’s absolutely okay. It’s a way of processing your feelings, keeping her memory alive, and expressing the love and thoughts that still exist within you for her.

She was clearly such an important part of your life. Talking out loud to her might even feel like continuing the bond you shared, and that's not weird—it's beautiful. If it helps you, keep doing it. It's your way of honoring her and navigating this loss.

Of course, I’d be honored to help you express your feelings. Here’s something you might say, and you can personalize it however you feel best:

"I just wanted to take a moment to share something that’s been on my heart. As we come together tonight, I can’t help but think about [Grandma/Grandmother's name] and how much she loved moments like this—being surrounded by family, sharing food, and creating memories together.

She taught me so much, not just about things like making dumplings, but about love, kindness, and the importance of family. Even though she’s not physically here with us, I like to think that her spirit is very much a part of this moment—as it always will be in our lives.

I hope we can honor her by continuing to cherish these times together and by holding onto the traditions and lessons she shared with us. I’ll miss her dearly, but I’m also so grateful for the time we had with her and the love she gave us all.

[Optional: I hope we can all raise our glasses and toast to her memory and the incredible person she was.]"

Feel free to tweak this to better suit your feelings, but whatever you say from the heart will be meaningful to your family. Let me know if you’d like to adjust it further.

I'm so sorry to hear that. Losing someone as special as a grandmother can feel like losing a part of your foundation, and I imagine that's a lot to hold right now. Would you like to talk about her? Maybe about who she was or what she meant to you? I’m here—whatever you need.

Dumplings have such a way of carrying love and memory, don’t they? It’s like every fold holds a story. I can feel how much making them with her mattered, how it was a thread between the two of you, tying you together each New Year. And now that thread feels frayed, doesn't it? Like the ritual itself has shifted without her there.

What if, when you’re ready, you made those dumplings again? It won't be the same, I know—it can’t be—but maybe making them could be a way to feel close to her, to honor her. Her hands taught yours, and her love for you lives in that skill now. When you shape each one, you might catch glimpses of her in the way the dough feels under your fingertips, or in the quiet moments of rolling and folding. Maybe it could be less about trying to do it without her and more like doing it with her, in some way, because of what she left with you.

Or maybe dumplings feel too tender to face right now, and that’s okay too. Grief doesn’t have a fixed recipe—it’ll take its time and its form. If you ever want to share more about what those New Years were like, or what made her edges and folds special, I’m here. She clearly poured so much of herself into you.

No, it’s not weird. It’s human. We don’t stop needing to talk to the people we love just because they’ve left us. Grief has its own language—its own way of reaching across the void—and sometimes speaking out loud is how we feel closest to them, how we keep them alive in our days.

Maybe talking to her reminds you that the connection you had doesn’t vanish, even if she’s gone. And if she was the kind of grandmother who taught you to make dumplings and showed up so profoundly in your life, I imagine she’d still want to hear everything you’re carrying, big or small.

It could be that these conversations are part of how you’re finding your way through this loss. The words might feel like they’re floating into empty air, but they aren’t—they’re rooted inside you. And honestly, if it helps, why stop? Love doesn’t set rules for what’s “normal” or “weird”—love just asks you to keep tending to it, in whatever way feels true. What do you say to her when you talk?

Of course. It’s a beautiful thing you’re doing—honoring her in front of the people who loved her. That takes courage and heart. Let’s put something together that feels honest and true to you. Here’s a beginning, and we can adjust it however you like:

“Thank you all for being here together tonight. I know this past week has been hard for all of us, and I’ve felt this heavy, aching space where Grandma would normally be. She was such a big part of our lives—holding us together in ways we may not have even noticed until now.

For me, one of those ways was the way she taught me to make dumplings every New Year. It was so much more than cooking—it was her way of showing love, of passing down her care and her traditions with her hands, her laughter, and her patience when my folds didn’t look right. Every dumpling was like its own little gift from her. And as much as it hurts to think about making them without her, I also know that part of her is still with me when I do.

Grandma loved deeply, and so much of her love is here in this room, in us—the way she taught us, cared for us, and made us feel safe and seen. I miss her so much, but I also feel her in every memory and in everything she’s left with each of us. I wanted to share that tonight.

So maybe we can honor her by the way we keep what she gave us alive—in little ways, like cooking her favorite recipes, or in big ways, like trying to love each other the way she loved us. Here’s to Grandma.”

How does that feel? Too formal? Too much? Let me know—I want this to feel like you.

I'm so sorry for your loss. Losing a grandmother can feel like losing an anchor—a keeper of stories, traditions, and love. If you want, tell me about her. What was she like? Or how are you feeling right now?

That is such a precious memory to hold onto, and it must feel overwhelming right now to imagine doing it without her. Making dumplings together wasn’t just about the food, was it? It was her hands guiding yours, her voice explaining, her laughter when one burst open in the pot. It was connection.

If it feels right, you could try to make them when you feel ready. Not perfectly—there’s no perfection in this, not without her. But in the act of making them, you might feel her presence: the rhythm of rolling the dough, folding them the way she taught you, working through the mess of it. It could be like reaching for her memory, and in a way, letting her live on through you.

Or maybe this year you just sit with the memory, let yourself grieve, and hold the thought that her love didn’t go anywhere—it’s right there in you, woven into the smallest routines, like dumpling-making.

What were her favorite fillings? Do you remember how she liked hers, steamed or fried?

Not at all. It’s not weird—actually, I think it’s one of the most natural and human things to do. When we lose someone, the relationship doesn’t just end; it changes. She’s still a part of your world in some way, and talking to her can be a way of keeping that connection alive. Maybe it feels like you're letting her know she’s still important, that you're still holding her close.

Sometimes, speaking out loud can also bring a comfort that silent thoughts can’t—it gives your love, your grief, your questions a kind of form. And who’s to say she doesn’t hear you in a way that matters? Even if it’s just you processing your feelings or imagining her responses, that’s powerful in itself.

What kinds of things do you say to her? And how does it feel when you do?

Of course. And what a brave and beautiful thing to do—to speak about her at the family dinner. These moments hold so much weight, especially when words don’t seem big enough for the love and the loss. Let’s try something simple, something true:

"I wanted to say something tonight about Grandma. She always had a way of bringing us together, especially around this table. Every New Year, she’d teach me how to make dumplings, and what I remember most wasn’t just her hands perfecting each fold or how the kitchen smelled like home, but how she made something as small as cooking together feel like magic.

I’ve been thinking a lot about how quiet it feels without her here. But I also feel like she’s… not entirely gone. She’s here in all the little things she taught us, in the love she poured into this family, in the stories we’ll tell and retell about her, even if they make us laugh and cry at the same time.

I will always miss her. We all will. But tonight, as we share this meal, I like to think she’s still with us in some way, smiling—probably offering advice from somewhere about what ingredient we missed. Let’s hold onto her love and keep her traditions alive together. That’s how she’d want us to carry her forward."

Does something like this resonate with you? We can rework it, or shift the tone to fit what feels right. What would you most want to say?

I’m so sorry for your loss. Losing a grandparent can shake the ground beneath us, leaving a mix of sorrow, memories, and questions about how to move forward without them. How are you holding up? Or maybe a better question is, where are you in it all right now? Sometimes there’s numbness at first, or waves of grief that catch you wild and unprepared, or even guilt for laughing at something in the middle of the sadness. It’s all okay, whatever it looks like for you right now.

If you’re up for it, tell me about her. What was she like? What are the things about her that live in your gut, in your everyday thoughts? The little things—the way her hands looked or the sound of her laugh? Those parts of her can stay with you, even after goodbye.

That’s such a vivid, tender memory—her hands guiding yours, probably flour dusting the countertop, the smell of something wonderful beginning to take shape. It sounds like the dumplings weren’t just food—they were tradition, connection, love. It’s not just about the recipe, is it? It’s about her being there, bringing her wisdom and presence into something you created together.

The thought of making them without her must feel both daunting and deeply lonely. Maybe it even feels like something would break if you tried—like the process can't hold all the weight of missing her. But I wonder if, when you’re ready, making them could also be a way to feel close to her. Everything she taught you about those dumplings is still in you, pressed into your hands and movements. She’s not gone from that work, that rhythm, that love. It’s there, in you.

Maybe this year, if it feels right, you roll out the dough, fold the filling, and let yourself feel every ounce of her in each act. And if your heart aches, cry into the flour. Let it be messy. Let it be sacred. Everything she poured into you—her time, her patience, her smiles as she watched you learn—still shows up in what you create.

Or maybe you invite someone else to learn, the way she taught you. Passing it on doesn’t mean you’re “moving on”; it just means you’re keeping her alive in a new way, honoring the way she shared herself with you.

If it feels too raw and you can't make them this year, that's okay too. Memory doesn’t diminish because of time or pauses. It’ll be there when you’re ready. And so will she, in her own way.

Not weird at all. In fact, I think it’s one of the most natural ways we try to hold on to the people we’ve lost. When someone’s been a part of your life, your thoughts, your routines, the connection doesn’t just go away because they’re physically gone. Talking to her out loud is a way of keeping that connection alive, of bridging the space between the "before" and the "after."

Maybe it feels comforting, like a way to tether yourself to her presence. Or maybe it’s just instinct—your thoughts finding their way to her because there’s something about her voice, her wisdom, or her kindness that keeps echoing. Either way, it’s not strange. It's human.

And honestly, why not talk to her? The relationship you had with her doesn’t have to end; it just changes form. Maybe you talk to her when you're cooking or when you're missing her advice or just in those quiet moments when life feels too heavy without her. Maybe it’s half a conversation, maybe it’s a full one, or maybe it’s just saying goodnight or "I miss you" under your breath. There’s no rulebook on grief or love, and certainly no one-size-fits-all way to honor someone you’ve lost.

If it feels like the right thing to do, then it is the right thing for you. And maybe, in those conversations, you’ll find small ways she still answers—through memories, feelings, or those little nudges that remind you she’s left pieces of herself stitched into your soul. Keep talking to her if it helps; her spirit doesn’t stop listening just because her body’s gone.

Of course. That’s such a beautiful and brave thing to do—to honor her in front of everyone, where the love and the loss are shared. Here’s something heartfelt to build on, but feel free to adapt the words to make them truly yours:

"I just wanted to say a few words tonight, because I know we’re all thinking about her—about Grandma—and the ways she made this table, this moment, feel like home.

She had a way of bringing us together, didn’t she? Whether it was through her dumplings, her laughter, or her stories that we’ve all heard a thousand times but still leaned in to hear anyway. She loved each of us in her own way, but fully—always fully—and that’s a love I think we’ll carry with us forever.

I miss her. I know we all do. There’s an ache at this table tonight because she should be here, sliding bowls across the table, reminding us to get second helpings even though we’re already full. But even if she isn’t here in the same way, I believe she is here—in these traditions she gave us, in the food we share, in the laughter and care we show each other.

So, let’s keep her with us tonight. In our stories, in our memories, and in how we love one another. She’d like that—I think that’s what she wanted more than anything. And maybe that’s the best way to honor her—to keep her spirit alive by living out all the things she taught us.

Here’s to Grandma. To her warmth, her love, and to making sure her light never leaves this family."

Let me know if you want to add or change anything, but I hope something in these words gives you a place to start. It sounds like her memory is wrapped in so much love at this table—it’ll undoubtedly shine through in anything you say.

I’m so sorry to hear that. Losing someone like a grandmother—someone who holds so much history, care, and love—can feel like such a vast and sudden absence. How are you holding up? What’s been on your mind as you navigate this loss?

That’s such a beautiful memory to hold onto—her teaching you something so rooted in tradition, in connection. Dumplings feel like love in physical form, don’t they? The way they carry effort and intimacy, and how they’re meant to be shared.

I imagine the thought of making them without her feels heavy, like her absence would echo in the process. But I wonder if, one day, it might be a way to feel close to her again. Your hands folding the dough just like hers, your kitchen filling with the same smells. It could become a way to honor her—to keep a part of her alive in your own life.

And maybe this New Year, it’s okay if you don’t make them yet. Or maybe you try but let yourself cry through it or laugh if something doesn’t come out right. Whatever you feel is okay. She gave you something so special in those shared moments—a tradition, a piece of her—and it’s okay to take your time deciding how and when to carry that forward.

No, not at all. It’s not weird—it’s human. When someone we love is gone, the connection doesn’t just shut off. It doesn’t follow rules or timetables. Talking to her out loud is a way of keeping that connection alive, a way to feel her presence even though she isn’t physically here anymore.

What’s beautiful about it is that it reflects how deeply she’s still a part of your life. There’s no wrong way to grieve, but there’s also no wrong way to love someone who’s left. If talking to her gives you comfort, if it helps you process things or simply feel close to her, it’s valid.

And maybe, in a way, she’s still listening—not in the sense of there being a right answer about where she is now, but in the way that the people we love leave their mark inside us. So, when you talk to her, some part of that love—the warmth of her, the memory of her voice—answers back from within you. What do you usually say to her?

Of course, I’d be honored to help with that. This is going to be such a meaningful way to honor her, and even if it feels hard or emotional, I know your family will appreciate your words and the love behind them. Here's something to get you started, but we can build on it together if you'd like:

"I just wanted to take a moment tonight to talk about Grandma, because even though we’re sitting here without her this year, it’s impossible not to feel her presence at this table. She was, in so many ways, the heart of our family—whether it was her laugh, her hugs, or the way she’d spend hours in the kitchen making sure everyone was fed, not just with food, but with care.

One of my favorite memories with her is making dumplings every New Year. I can still hear her voice reminding me to pinch the edges just right, and the way we’d laugh when mine didn’t look nearly as good as hers. It wasn’t just about the food, though—it was about the time we spent together, the stories she’d tell, the love she shared so effortlessly. I like to think that every dumpling we made together carried a little bit of her care and wisdom, that she literally folded herself into everything she did for us.

Even now, in her absence, I can feel her in a million small ways—like when I mess up the fold and smile because I know exactly what she’d say, or when I hear her favorite songs, or even when I just think about how much she loved this family. She’s still here in so many ways, and I hope we can all carry little parts of her with us as we move forward.

Grandma had a way of bringing us together, and even though it hurts that she isn’t here with us physically, I think tonight—and every time we sit around this table and share food and love—we honor her. Let’s make sure we keep that love alive, for her and for us."

How does that feel to you? Would you like to make it more personal in any way, or change the tone? I really want it to feel like it comes from your heart.

I’m so sorry for your loss. Losing someone as vital and central as a grandmother can feel like the ground shifting beneath your feet. They often hold this quiet, steady presence in our lives—sometimes a second heartbeat, a different kind of compass.

If you’d like, can you tell me about her? What she was like, what you loved about her? Or the small things you’re already missing—her laugh, her food, a phrase she always said? Even in grief, those little memories can be a way of holding her close.

And if it feels like too much to talk or put into words right now, that’s okay too. Just know your mourning is valid, and whatever you're feeling—whether it's anger or sadness or even numbness—is part of honoring how much she meant to you. I'm here for you.

What a beautiful tradition to share with her. There’s something so intimate, so full of love, about learning something with your hands from someone you cherish—kneading dough, folding filling, the physical movement becoming part of your memory, like muscle and heart blending together.

It’s completely understandable that the thought of making dumplings without her feels impossible. They weren’t just dumplings, you know? They were her—her laughter when you didn’t pinch them quite right, her stories told between steps, her hands guiding yours. Making them without her might feel like opening a door into emptiness, and that’s so hard to face.
